raw_case_text:
A male, 31-years-old patient, with no significant medical history, presented in February 2011 with a cellulitis-like plaque on the right inner thigh (10 cm diameter) that, in about 12 hours, extended to almost the entire thigh. He was living in a Romanian suburban area (near Bucharest) and had a pet dog. The patient denied recent or past travel abroad, except for France (Paris) for a weekend, 4 months earlier (in October). The putative diagnosis at that time was cellulitis, and antibiotic treatment was started with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (for 5 days). All symptoms subsided rapidly within 24-48 hours.
One week later the patient developed severe muscle pain in the lower right leg, and after a further two days he noticed a similar cellulitis-like plaque as before (red, edematous, warm with imprecise limits) in the popliteal region, with rapid extension to the adjacent areas, associated with impaired walking ability due to extensive edema. Doppler ultrasound showed no signs of thrombosis in the right leg. Laboratory investigations showed mild eosinophilia (7.2%; normal range 0-7%). All other investigations including complete blood count, sedimentation rate, urinalysis, and liver and renal function tests were normal. Because of the severity of symptoms, treatment with the macrolide antibiotic azithromycin and the low-molecular-weight heparin enoxaparin was administered for 7 days. Again the symptoms resolved quickly and completely.
After about two further weeks, the patient developed similar but less severe lesions on the lower right part of the abdomen that were again associated with muscle pain (Figure 1(a)).
Infectious disease screening was performed and showed positive serology for Echinococcus (E.) granulosus IgG (ELISA) and negative tests for Borrelia burgdorferi, Toxoplasma gondii, Toxocara canis, Trichinella spiralis, EBV, CMV, HBV, HCV, and HIV. Abdominal ultrasound and chest radiography were normal.
Because of the eosinophilia and the positive E. granulosus serology, a parasitological cause was suspected and albendazole treatment was started (800 mg/day). During antiparasitic therapy, the inflammatory abdominal plaque resolved, but a nodule developed deep in the subcutaneous tissue (Figure 1(b)). The nodule was excised, and all signs of infection including the eosinophilia subsided, and no further symptoms developed (Figure 1(c)).
The excised material was investigated histopathologically using hematoxylin-eosin (HE), Giemsa, and Masson's trichrome stains, periodic acid-Schiff reaction, and immunohistochemistry for IgE (Figure 2). The histopathology was similar to that described for subcutaneous dirofilariasis in previous reports. The parasite showed the typical features of a nongravid female D. repens. The most indicative structures were the external longitudinal ridges, leading to a cogwheel-like appearance in the transverse sections (Figures 2(a), 2(b), and 2(c)). Further typical features were the thick cuticula and the well-developed musculature (Figures 2(a) and 2(c)). Around the parasite a marked inflammatory reaction had developed (Figures 2(d) and 2(e)). The histological slides showed numerous eosinophils, neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages. (Figures 2(d) and 2(e)). Occasionally, eosinophils and neutrophils, partly with pycnotic nuclei, were seen on the surface of the parasite (Figures 2(d) and 2(e)). Many IgE-positive plasma cells were present in the infiltration and near to the surface of the parasite (Figure 2(f)).
To confirm the morphological diagnosis, DNA was isolated from the tissue sample embedded in paraffin wax and a PCR targeting the mitochondrial 12S rRNA was performed as described before. Sequence analysis of the PCR product showed the highest similarity to Italian isolates of D. repens, thus confirming the morphological identification of our isolate as D. repens.  
Serum samples were investigated retrospectively for antifilarial antibodies using an ELISA composed of D. immitis antigen. The test was positive as expected. In addition, the presence of antibodies against E. granulosus was confirmed by ELISA and indirect hemagglutination, but not by a western blot confirmation test. The patient was thoroughly screened for signs of an Echinococcus infection by sonography and CT scans, but no indications of a hydatid cyst were found.
In order to exclude the patient's dog as a source of (further) D. repens infections, blood samples were obtained and investigated for microfilaria using Giemsa stain and PCR. No microfilaria or filarial DNA was found.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old Romanian man presented with recurrent migratory cellulitis-like erythematous plaques and myalgia affecting the right thigh, right popliteal region, and right lower abdomen over a 1-month period.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In February 2011, the patient developed a 10-cm cellulitis-like plaque on his right inner thigh that expanded across the thigh within 12 hours and resolved within 24-48 hours on amoxicillin-clavulanate. One week later, he developed severe right lower leg myalgia and a warm edematous plaque in the popliteal fossa impairing ambulation, which resolved with 7 days of azithromycin and enoxaparin. Two weeks later, a third erythematous plaque with muscle pain appeared on the right lower abdomen.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history; lived in a suburban area near Bucharest, Romania, owned a pet dog, and had traveled only to Paris for a weekend 4 months earlier.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for migratory erythematous edematous plaques, localized myalgia, and transient gait impairment.

objective.physical_examination: Successive warm, red, edematous cellulitis-like plaques on the right inner thigh, right popliteal region, and right lower abdomen, the latter evolving during albendazole therapy into a deep subcutaneous nodule.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed mild eosinophilia (7.2%; normal 0-7%) with normal CBC, ESR, urinalysis, and liver and renal function tests. Right leg venous Doppler ultrasound, chest X-ray, and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Initial screening ELISA and IHA for Echinococcus granulosus IgG were positive, whereas E. granulosus Western blot and serologies for Borrelia, Toxoplasma, Toxocara, Trichinella, EBV, CMV, HBV, HCV, and HIV were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracoabdominal CT scans showed no hydatid cysts. Excisional biopsy histopathology (H&E, Giemsa, Masson's trichrome, PAS, and IgE IHC) of the right lower abdominal subcutaneous nodule revealed a nongravid female Dirofilaria repens nematode with characteristic external longitudinal cuticular ridges (cogwheel transverse appearance) and well-developed musculature surrounded by eosinophils, neutrophils, and IgE-positive plasma cells. Paraffin-tissue PCR and sequencing of the mitochondrial 12S rRNA gene confirmed Dirofilaria repens (retrospective D. immitis-antigen antifilarial ELISA was also positive).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis caused by Dirofilaria repens with cross-reactive false-positive Echinococcus granulosus ELISA/IHA serologies (hydatid disease excluded by negative Western blot and CT imaging), definitively confirmed by histopathology and 12S rRNA PCR sequencing. During empirical oral albendazole therapy (800 mg/day), the migrating worm localized into a subcutaneous abdominal nodule that was curatively excised, resulting in complete resolution of symptoms and eosinophilia.
